newsitem.title: INDIA: Eagle Star welcomes India insurance sector reform.
newsitem.headline: Eagle Star welcomes India insurance sector reform.

text.p: British insurance group Eagle Star said on Saturday India's decision to open pension and health insurance to the private sector is a step in the right direction towards attracting foreign investment.
"The announcement is the first reaffirmation that India remains an important (foreign) investment destination," a company statement said.

"The Indian economy will benefit substantially by the opening up of the insurance sector through better channeling of funds for productive purposes," Tom Naskret, chief executive (international development) of Eagle Star, said at a briefing.
Eagle Star, a 100 percent subsidiary of B.A.T Industries Plc, opened its second office in New Delhi. It has a office in Bombay.

Last month, Finance Minister P. Chidambaram, while unveiling the budget for 1997/98 (April-March), announced that India would allow private investors into pensions and health insurance by permitting joint ventures with its two state-run monopolies, Life Insurance Corp and General Insurance Corp.
He said only Indian firms, controlled by Indians and having a majority Indian ownership, would be permitted to enter the health insurance business.
"We are anxious to commit funds in India," James Robertson, country manager of Eagle Star, told Reuters. He did not give details.
Robertson said the Delhi office's function would be to accurately assess the insurance market in India and serve the non-resident Indians policy holders.
Naskret said India was one of the most under-insured markets, with $5 per capita spending on insurance premiums compared with $30 for Thailand and $407 in Taiwan.
"In India, premiums account for ony 0.58 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) compared to 5.1 percent in the United States," Naskret said. "So India has a lot of potential."
Eagle Star had operations in India until 1972, when the insurance companies were nationalised.
"So in many ways we are seeking to return to a market we did not want to leave," Naskret added.
